dedupe_keys.name: catastrophic electricity loss and the food supply chain system dynamics model validated on the 2019 venezuela blackouts

description: This case study builds a system dynamics model of how a prolonged, widespread loss of electricity would disrupt the food supply chain. The authors, at the Alliance to Feed the Earth in Disasters, the University of Canterbury and the University of Cologne, published it in an open-access journal article with the model released as open source. The model links five infrastructures, the electric grid, liquid fuels, the internet, transport and the workforce, to food supply, and was validated against the 2019 Venezuelan blackouts. It was then used to explore a large cyberattack on the US grid and a high-altitude electromagnetic pulse (HEMP) event. Coverage is the United States for the scenarios, with Venezuela for validation. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Caveats: the extreme scenarios are hypothetical, and results assume equitable food distribution. The study found that a cyberattack with recovery within weeks or months would cut food consumption substantially but still allow adequate calories for everyone, whereas a year-long recovery from a HEMP event affecting most of the continental United States could lead to famine. Simulation uses: an open cross-sector model for cascading failure from power loss to food supply, applicable to solar storms and pandemics. Related records: the labour shortage resilience study (case_study-us-covid-labour-shortage-food-energy-water-resilience) looks at another cross-sector shock.
